title: Designing a study
summary: Turn a topic into a research question GCAM can answer, design a Reference and levers, choose price or quantity policies, and plan the uncertainty analysis before you run anything.
outcomes: Turn a broad topic into a question with a decision, a metric and a comparison
Design a scenario matrix with a Reference, levers, policies and sensitivity cases
Choose between a carbon price and an emissions constraint for a given question
Write an uncertainty plan and a validity argument before running GCAM
narration_en: A good GCAM study answers one clear question. A topic, such as electric vehicles in Saudi Arabia, is not yet a question. A question names a decision, a metric and a comparison: for example, how much would cheaper batteries reduce transport carbon dioxide in 2050 compared with a carbon price that costs the same. Next comes the scenario logic. The Reference run keeps today's policies and assumptions. Levers change one assumption at a time, such as vehicle costs, load factors or the value of time. Policies are added on top, either as a price on carbon, where the model finds the emissions, or as a cap on emissions, where the model finds the price. Then, before you run anything, plan the uncertainty: which inputs are most uncertain, what ranges you will test, and whether you need a small sensitivity analysis or a full ensemble. Finally, write down why anyone should believe your results: calibration, comparison with history, and comparison with other models.
narration_ar: الدراسة الجيدة باستخدام GCAM تجيب عن سؤال واحد واضح. فالموضوع، مثل المركبات الكهربائية في المملكة العربية السعودية، ليس سؤالًا بعد. السؤال يحدد قرارًا ومقياسًا ومقارنة: مثلًا، كم ستخفض البطاريات الأرخص انبعاثات ثاني أكسيد الكربون من النقل عام 2050 مقارنةً بسعر للكربون يكلّف القدر نفسه. ثم يأتي منطق السيناريوهات. فسيناريو الأساس يُبقي السياسات والافتراضات الحالية. والروافع تغيّر افتراضًا واحدًا في كل مرة، مثل تكاليف المركبات أو معامل الإشغال أو قيمة الوقت. وتُضاف السياسات فوق ذلك، إما سعرًا للكربون يجد النموذج عنده الانبعاثات، وإما سقفًا للانبعاثات يجد النموذج عنده السعر. وقبل أن تشغّل أي شيء، خطِّط لعدم اليقين: ما المدخلات الأكثر غموضًا، وما النطاقات التي ستختبرها، وهل تحتاج تحليل حساسية صغيرًا أم مجموعة كاملة من التشغيلات. وأخيرًا، اكتب لماذا ينبغي لأي أحد أن يصدّق نتائجك: المعايرة، والمقارنة بالتاريخ، والمقارنة بالنماذج الأخرى.

diagram.title: The study design cycle
diagram.caption: Each box is a decision you write down before running GCAM; validity feeds back into the question.

nodes.label: Question
nodes.detail: A topic becomes a question when it names a decision, a metric (for example 2050 transport CO2) and a comparison (against Reference or another policy).

nodes.label: Reference
nodes.detail: The counterfactual world: a stated SSP, current policies, default technology assumptions. Report it in full.

nodes.label: Levers
nodes.detail: Vehicle costs, load factors, share-weight paths, value of time, fuel prices: each changed alone first.

nodes.label: Policies
nodes.detail: A carbon price (model finds emissions) or a constraint (model finds the price); standards as credit markets.

nodes.label: Uncertainty plan
nodes.detail: Choose uncertain inputs, ranges and method: one-at-a-time sensitivity, a factorial matrix, or an ensemble with scenario discovery.

nodes.label: Validity
nodes.detail: Calibration, hindcast against recent history, and benchmarking against other models and the AR6 database.

tour.text: Start with a question that names a decision, a metric and a comparison.
Define the Reference, then change one lever at a time.
Add policies as a price or a quantity, depending on what your question asks.
Plan the uncertainty analysis before running: inputs, ranges and method.
Argue validity, and refine the question if the design cannot answer it.

sections.heading: From topic to question
sections.html:
"EVs in Saudi Arabia" is a topic. A research question names a decision, a metric and a comparison:

WeakStrongWhy stronger
What is the future of EVs in KSA?How much do 2060 Saudi transport CO2 emissions differ between a ZEV sales standard and a carbon price that achieves the same 2040 car-emission cut, and at what cost?Decision (instrument choice), metric (CO2, cost), comparison (equal-effort policies)
Can aviation be decarbonised?At what CO2 price does bio-jet with CCS beat DAC offsets for Gulf aviation residuals, and how sensitive is it to biomass supply?A threshold and a sensitivity, both computable
Will rail help freight?How much do Saudi freight emissions fall by 2050 if rail's share-weight doubles, and how much of that survives a freight logit exponent of −4 instead of −2?Separates the policy effect from a structural assumption

sections.heading: Scenario logic: Reference, levers and policies
sections.html:
Every GCAM study compares runs that differ in a controlled way. Three layers are enough for most transport questions:

  1. Background world: an SSP (population, GDP, the matching transport file transportation_UCD_SSP1/3/5.xml; SSP2 uses CORE) and current policies.
  2. Levers: the assumptions your question is about — BEV cost, share-weight path, load factors, speed of rail, a fuel technology you add.
  3. Policies: none, a carbon price, an emissions constraint (net zero), a standard (ZEV credits, fuel quantity cap).

Hold everything else at Reference. If two things change at once, you cannot say which caused the difference.

sections.heading: Policies: price or quantity?
sections.html:
GCAM implements a carbon price (fixedTax), an emissions constraint (constraint, for which the model solves the shadow price), and portfolio standards (credit markets). A price fixes cost and lets emissions follow; a cap fixes emissions and lets the price follow. For comparisons of instruments, match them on one dimension: either equal emissions (then compare cost) or equal price (then compare emissions). Go 2 showed that a cap and a price can be two doors to the same room; in a study you must say which door you used.

InstrumentYou specifyGCAM returnsGood for

Policy portfolio standarda credit market and its constraintcredit price, compliance mixZEV mandates, fuel standards
Share-weight or cost changean assumptionuptake"what if technology X were cheaper/preferred?" (not a policy!)

sections.heading: Plan the uncertainty before you run
sections.html:
Write a table of 3–6 uncertain inputs, each with a low, central and high value and a source. Choose a design: one-at-a-time (cheap, misses interactions), full factorial (clean, explodes in size), or a Latin-hypercube sample (efficient for many inputs, analysed with regression or scenario discovery). sections.heading: Validity: why should anyone believe it?
sections.html:
• Calibration check: base-year outputs reproduce IEA energy by fuel (they should, by construction — so this checks the data, not the model).
  • Hindcast: run from 2015 with observed prices and compare 2021–2024 with data you did not calibrate to (e.g. Saudi gasoline demand after the 2016 and 2018 price reforms; IEA EV sales).
  • Benchmark: compare your Reference with other models in the AR6 database or EMF studies for the same region and variables.
  • Face validity: show results to people who know the sector; implausible numbers usually reveal an input error.

callouts.title: Why this matters
callouts.html: Four uncertain inputs with three values each make 81 GCAM runs. Add three policies and you have 243. At two hours a run on four cores, that is about five days of computing — before a single one has failed to solve. Design is the step where you decide which runs answer the question and which only fill a hard drive.

callouts.title: Worked calculation
callouts.html:
How many runs, and how long?

  1. Full factorial: 3 SSPs × 2 BEV cost levels × 2 share-weight paths × 3 policies = 36 runs.
  2. At about 2 hours per run (machine-dependent; check your own) and 4 runs in parallel: 36 × 2 ÷ 4 = 18 hours.
  3. Add a 3-level freight exponent test only for the central SSP and two policies: + 3 × 2 = 6 runs.
  4. Allow 10 % for failed runs and re-runs: about 46 runs in total.

Answer: ≈ 46 runs, a day of computing — feasible; the 243-run version is not

callouts.title: Pitfall
callouts.html: Calling an assumption a policy. Setting BEV share-weights to 1 makes BEVs popular; it does not say which policy would make them popular, or what it would cost. If your scenario is "high EV preference", name it as an assumption and, if you can, pair it with a policy (credit standard, subsidy via input-subsidy) whose cost GCAM reports.

callouts.title: Research note
callouts.html: Pre-register your design. Before the first run, write down the scenarios, the uncertain ranges and the figures you will make (the kit's templates/research_proposal.md has the headings). It protects you from running until something looks interesting, and it makes the honest "what the model cannot tell us" section much easier to write.

callouts.title: Try it
callouts.html:
1. Rewrite this into a strong question: "Hydrogen trucks in the Gulf". Name the decision, metric and comparison.
  2. Your design has 2 SSPs × 3 BEV costs × 2 exponents × 3 policies. How many runs? Which factor would you drop first, and why?

takeaways: A question names a decision, a metric and a comparison
Change one lever at a time against a fully described Reference
A price fixes cost and finds emissions; a cap fixes emissions and finds the price
Plan inputs, ranges and method for uncertainty before the first run
State why results are credible: calibration, history and other models

quiz.q: Which of these is a research question rather than a topic?
options: How much would 30% cheaper BEVs cut 2050 transport CO2 relative to Reference?
quiz.explain: It names a lever, a metric and a comparison.

quiz.q: You must meet a fixed emissions target and want to know its cost. Use…
quiz.explain: A constraint fixes the quantity; GCAM finds the shadow price.

quiz.q: Why change one lever at a time first?
options: So each effect can be attributed
quiz.explain: One-at-a-time runs show what each assumption does before combinations.

quiz.q: Scenario discovery is most useful when…
options: You have an ensemble and an outcome of interest
You only want the base year
quiz.explain: It searches an ensemble for input ranges that explain outcomes.
